html:
The coins of the kingdom of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, struck in gold, silver and bronze from about 270 CE to the 7th century. They were the first coins made in Africa south of Egypt.

The first known issues come from King Endubis. Aksum then controlled trade between the Roman world, Arabia and India through its Red Sea port of Adulis, and coins helped it take part. Gold coins were made to a weight close to Roman ones and carried Greek writing, the trade language of the Red Sea, so foreign merchants could use them. Bronze coins for use at home often carried Ge'ez writing instead.

The coins tell a story of faith. Early ones show the crescent and disc of the old gods. After King Ezana became Christian, around 330, the cross replaced them, making Aksum one of the first states to put a cross on its coins. It is key evidence for when Aksum adopted Christianity.

Minting stopped in the 7th century as Red Sea trade shifted after the rise of Islam.
sum: The coins of the kingdom of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, struck in gold, silver and bronze from about 270 CE to the 7th century. They were the first coins made in Africa south of Egypt.
